title: Inline Assembly
description: Write low-level assembly code directly in BPL. Learn Intel, AT&T, and LLVM IR syntax for maximum control.
objectives: Understand when to use inline assembly
Write Intel and AT&T syntax assembly
Pass values between BPL and assembly
Use LLVM IR for advanced operations

sections.title: Why Inline Assembly?
sections.content:
Sometimes you need to go lower than high-level code:

**Use cases:**
- 🚀 Performance-critical code
- 🔧 Hardware access (I/O ports, special registers)
- 🔐 Cryptographic operations (AES instructions)
- 📊 SIMD/vector operations
- 🖥️ OS kernel development

⚠️ **Warning:** Assembly is:
- Not portable (CPU-specific)
- Hard to debug
- Easy to break

Use only when absolutely necessary!

sections.title: AT&T Syntax

lineExplanations.8: % prefix for registers, l suffix for 32-bit.

sections.title: Intel vs AT&T Syntax
sections.content:
| Feature | Intel | AT&T |
|---------|-------|------|
| Order | dest, src | src, dest |
| Registers | eax | %eax |
| Size suffix | None | l (32), q (64) |
| Immediate | 42 | $42 |
| Memory | [eax] | (%eax) |

**Intel:** `mov eax, 42` (move 42 into eax)

**AT&T:** `movl $42, %eax` (move 42 into eax)

BPL handles the variable binding, so you mostly just use:
- `(var)` - read variable
- `(=var)` - write to variable

sections.title: Assembly Guidelines
sections.content:
**DO:**
✅ Use for performance-critical inner loops
✅ Document thoroughly what the code does
✅ Test on all target platforms
✅ Keep assembly blocks small and focused
✅ Have a fallback pure-BPL implementation

**DON'T:**
❌ Use assembly as first solution
❌ Assume it's faster (compilers are good!)
❌ Use without measuring performance
❌ Write complex logic in assembly
❌ Forget about portability

sections.title: Variable Binding Summary
sections.content:
**Reading variables:**
```
(varname)       # Default constraint "r"
(varname: "r")  # Explicit register constraint
(varname: "m")  # Memory constraint
```

**Writing variables:**
```
(=varname)       # Default "=r"
(=varname: "=r") # Explicit output register
(=varname: "=m") # Output to memory
```

**Constraints:**
- `"r"` - any general register
- `"a"` - eax/rax
- `"b"` - ebx/rbx
- `"c"` - ecx/rcx
- `"d"` - edx/rdx
- `"m"` - memory location

sections.title: Practice: Swap Without Temp
sections.hint: Use Intel syntax. Load *a and *b, do three XOR operations, store back.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
sections.content:
✅ Use `asm("intel")`, `asm("att")`, or `asm("llvm")`

✅ Read variables: `(varname)` or `(varname: "constraint")`

✅ Write variables: `(=varname)` or `(=varname: "=constraint")`

✅ List clobbered registers: `[ "eax", "ebx" ]`

✅ Use **only when necessary** for performance/hardware

✅ **Document** and **test** thoroughly

✅ Keep assembly **small and focused**

questions.question: What does (=result) mean in inline assembly?
questions.explanation: The = prefix indicates an output (write) operand.

questions.question: What's the order in Intel syntax?
questions.explanation: Intel syntax uses destination, source order (mov eax, 5 moves 5 into eax).

questions.question: When should you use inline assembly?
options: Only when BPL can't express it
questions.explanation: Use assembly only when high-level code can't achieve what you need (hardware access, specific instructions).
